questions.question: What stats does the model actually use?
questions.answer: The simulator reads two numbers per team: its net rating and its win percentage, each against its own league [C1]. Every other stat it was offered carries zero weight [C1]. These two inputs are used as z-scores against the team's own league [C4]. The model uses these to estimate win probability and a rough point margin [C5]. One standard deviation of net rating moves the log-odds about 2.8 times as much as one standard deviation of win %, so net rating decides most matchups [C4].

questions.question: Why does the model only look at net rating and win percentage?
questions.answer: The simulator only looks at net rating and win percentage because every other stat it was offered carries zero weight [C1, C4]. The hist-v2 classifier gives non-zero weight to only two inputs: net rating and win %, each as a z-score against the team's own league [C2]. This means the model reads two numbers per team, which are its net rating and its win percentage [C1]. The simulator does not account for rosters, individual players, injuries, rest, trades during the season, playoff experience, coaching, rule changes beyond what shows up in the league averages, or how styles would match up [C5].

questions.question: Does it know which players were on each team?

questions.question: Why are teams from the 80s judged differently from modern teams?
questions.answer: The simulator reads each stat as a z-score to ensure teams from different eras compare fairly [C1]. Because raw numbers drift between eras, such as league offensive rating rising from about 105 to 108 points per 100 possessions in the late 1980s and 1990s to about 115 in the 2020s, a model reading raw numbers would judge an older team on a scale that moved [C1]. This would tilt evenly matched cross-era games toward modern teams [C1]. Instead, the simulator judges how many standard deviations a team was above or below the average of its own season's league [C1].
